text: Shall the measure creating a special parcel tax to fund grants for performing arts organizations, art projects, art organization operational and programmatic expenses and capital projects, community festivals, and administrative costs, with oversight by the City’s Civic Arts Commission, at a rate of $0.07 per square foot of improvements, estimated to generate approximately $6,300,000 annually and $84,800,000 over its twelve- year duration, be adopted?

analysis.title: Impartial Analysis
analysis.by: Farimah Faiz Brown, Berkeley City Attorney

text:
This measure was placed on the ballot by an initiative petition signed by the requisite number of registered voters in the City of Berkeley. It requires a majority vote for passage.
This measure would impose a special parcel tax to fund arts institutions and programs through grants. If adopted, the tax would be imposed starting January 1, 2027, at a rate of $0.07 per square foot of improvements on all properties, excluding properties (1) owned and occupied by low-income seniors or very low-income households; (2) owned by tax-exempt religious or educational organizations; (3) where at least 60% of units are designated affordable housing; or (4) that are transitional housing for people experiencing homelessness. The City estimates the tax would raise approximately $6,300,000 in the first year, and $84,800,000 over its 12-year duration.
Proceeds would be placed into a special fund and allocated as follows:

75% for performing arts organizations. Eligible organizations must demonst rate at least 3 consecutive years of providing live performances in Berkeley. The maximum grant would vary based on applicants’ annual operating expenses, but no more than $1,250,000. Funds could be used for operational and programmatic expenses such as wages, supplies and materials, and venue and equipment rentals, but not for long-term capital projects, fundraising or debt reduction. Applicants applying for awards greater than $100,000 must provide community benefits such as discounted programming.

5% for individual artist projects or art organization operational and programmatic expenses. The maximum grant would be $7,500 for individual artists and $25,000 per year for organizations. Individual applicants must be at least 18 years old, Berkeley residents, and not applying as a partnership, group, or collective. Full-time students, City employees, or individuals producing a festival would be ineligible.

10% for capital projects for arts organizations. The maximum grant would be $200,000 per project. Applicants must show they plan to acquire or construct a new asset, or improve or repair existing assets. Funds could not be used for regular programming or administrative costs unrelated to the capital project.
5% for community festivals, including art fairs, cultural celebrations, or other limited-time events. The maximum grant would be $25,000 per festival.

5% for grant program administrative costs. Requirements for eligibility and permissible uses of funds vary by program. Generally, organizational applicants must be Berkeley nonprofits. For-profit businesses and the City of Berkeley would be ineligible for grants and public or private school districts and organizations affiliated with the government or an educational institution such as the University of California would be ineligible for most grants. The City’s Civic Arts Commission would review and approve grant applications and adopt regulations to effectuate the purposes of the measure. Civic Arts Commission regulations and grant awards would be subject to City Council review and approval.
The City Council would not be able to amend the measure without voter approval, but could fix technical errors, clarify the calculation of the tax, or adopt regulations by majority vote.

Arts and culture are a critical part of what makes Berkeley a special place to live, and are central to Berkeley’s identity and values. Let’s keep it that way. Yes on Measure Y. YES on Y preserves Berkeley’s nonprofit performing arts theater, music, dance, and visual arts venues for children, adults, and seniors, maintaining Berkeley as an arts and cultural destination for generations to come. It also supports grants for individual artists from diverse backgrounds. YES on Y helps create a stronger economy and better quality of life in Berkeley. Berkeley’s creative economy supports 8,000 jobs, contributes $10 million in annual City revenue, and makes our downtown and neighborhoods more vibrant. Our arts organizations increase property values, attract new businesses, and bring patrons to support our restaurants, hotels, and other businesses.
YES on Y supports arts organizations still struggling to recover from the lingering impacts of the pandemic. Over the past few years, several beloved Berkeley arts organizations closed, and more could follow. We must support our arts organizations and artists and preserve Berkeley’s artistic and cultural legacy.
YES on Y protects the community benefits Berkeley’s arts institutions provide, including youth educational oppor t u nities, f ree public festivals and cult u ral performances, and discounts for residents and workers. YES on Y helps Berkeley stand up to a federal government intent on defunding the arts. Local communities like Berkeley are our last line of defense to protect freedom of speech and expression.
The Civic Arts Commission and regular audits will provide strict oversight to ensure Measure Y’s funds are spent as promised.
Endorsements: Berkeley Chamber of Commerce, State Senator Jesse Arreguín, Councilmembers Shoshana O’Keefe, Brent Blackaby, Susan Wengraf, Igor Tregub, and Mark Humbert, Ashkenaz Music & Dance Community Center, Berkeley Repertory Theatre, The Freight, Berkeley Ballet, Berkeley Playhouse, Shotgun Players, Berkeley Symphony, Cazadero Music Camp, The UC Theatre, and more.

text: It’s not a bailout—it’s a massive
annual
The sponsors designed this measure to favor their chances to obtain grants!

During the pandemic, the City of Berkeley provided emergency grants up to $180,000. Under Measure Y, grants of $1,250,000 can be awarded. This is far more than any of the qualified organizations net in an entire year of productions. Arts organizations will be compelled to focus on campaigning for grants.

Berkeley City Council members are allowed to accept up to $630 in gifts, per source annually, with no limit on total gifts. An endorsing council member reported receiving free tickets for three shows from the sponsor UC Theatre for whom he voted in favor of a $45,000 grant. Passing this measure creates a system where politicians can easily reward the organizations that pamper them.

True financial emergencies require belt-tightening. Yet, between 2021 and 2025, the Berkeley Repertory Theatre gave its two directors $50,000 raises, pushing their individual salaries past $350,000. If organizations can afford executive raises like this, there is no emergency.

Measure Y provides an excessive amount of funding because it was drafted without fiscal restraint. This tax will exacerbate our high cost of living and ultimately raise the rents for apartments, retail shops and industrials. It places the government over the patron.

strong: Vote no on Measure Y to save Berkeley taxpayers

text:
Over time, public tastes evolve. Some artistic endeavors f lourish while others lose favor. While the pandemic presented severe challenges for everyone, that crisis officially ended years ago. The arts organizations that weathered those years are now financially stable. What we are witnessing today is not an emergency—it is the natural shift in consumer demand.
When audiences change, organizations have two choices: adapt or ask for a government bailout.
Consider the contrasting approaches of two local institutions:

The Freight & Salvage recognized that its traditional folk music programming was no longer filling seats. By expanding their musical genres to match changing community tastes, Freight & Salvage brought in more than 66,500 ticket sales in 2025—demonstrating a healthy, resilient business model driven by audience support.

Berkeley Repertory Theatre, on the other hand, successfully navigated the pandemic by raising over $30 million in contributions. Yet in 2025, after shifting focus from works of broad artistic merit to niche political narratives, the Rep saw its program revenues plunge by more than $1,000,000. Taxpayers should not be forced to under write an organization’s decision to produce works that discourage paying audiences. City Hall should not have the power to overrule the choices of everyday arts patrons.
The measure lacks accountability. It includes no guardrails, sets out complex rules and sets no objective criteria for how tax dollars are awarded. Final approval rests with the City Council—whose members are legally permitted to accept gifts up to $630 from individual organizations without an aggregate cap.

This property tax hikes the cost of living for working families. A measure that rewards failing business strategies while leaving distribution open to political influence is bad policy. Keep the power where it belongs: with the audience.

text:
Measure Y is an investment in Berkeley’s quality of life, creative economy, and future. The arts celebrate humanity, create jobs and educational opportunities, maintain vibrant commercial corridors and neighborhoods, and bring people to local businesses.
Supporting Berkeley’s diverse arts ecosystem is a strong economic investment. Every ticket generates an additional $14-$16 for Berkeley’s economy. According to a 2025 study, arts organizations receiving City arts grants generated $137,400,000 in economic activity within Berkeley. Opponents falsely claim Berkeley’s arts sector has recovered from the pandemic. The data and our arts organizations’ experience say otherwise. Recovery has been uneven, fragile, and incomplete. Berkeley’s creative economy employment remains 17% below pre-pandemic levels. Nearly half of nonprofit arts organizations are operating at a deficit–with music, theater, and film/media organizations struggling most. That’s why Berkeley’s nonprofit arts organizations united to sponsor this citizen-led initiative. With clear guardrails, Measure Y establishes competitive grant programs supporting nonprofit arts organizations of all sizes, individual artists, community festivals, and cultural infrastructure. Grants are evaluated by panels of independent experts using established criteria, reviewed publicly, and are awarded by the Civic Arts Commission. Annual audits and financial reporting are required. Funds are legally restricted to specified purposes.
Measure Y exempts low-income seniors, very low-income households, tax-exempt religious and educational organizations, and affordable housing.
Berkeley’s creative economy employs thousands, generates millions in City revenue, strengthens businesses, provides arts education and free public events, and makes Berkeley a special place to live.
A Berkeley without the arts isn’t truly Berkeley
